periods.activity_title: A Land of Many Names: Opening the Inquiry
periods.section_anchor: Introduction — India as an ancient land with changing names
materials: Blackboard or chart paper
Physical map of the Indian Subcontinent (Fig. 5.2)
periods.visual_aids: Physical map of the Indian Subcontinent showing major rivers, mountains, and coasts

time_bands.activity: Students write down, individually and quickly, all the names they have ever heard used for India — in different languages, in songs, in official documents. Pairs then compare lists and note which names seem old and which seem recent.

Teacher displays the physical map of the Subcontinent and poses two driving questions that frame the chapter: 'How did the people who lived here name their own land?' and 'How did people from outside name it?' Students locate the Indus River, the Himalayas, Cape Kumari, and the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal on the map, noticing that the Subcontinent is bounded by water on three sides and mountains on one — a shape that would matter to name-givers.

Teacher introduces the idea that a 'name' is a form of evidence: it tells us who was naming, what they noticed, and when. Students sort their collected names from the opening task into two rough columns — 'names from inside India' and 'names from outside India' — and predict what kind of source might have preserved each.

Whole-class share-out: three or four pairs report one name each and the source they predicted. Teacher uses responses to preview the chapter's two organising sections without foreclosing the inquiry, leaving the sorting as an open hypothesis to be tested through the rest of the chapter.

periods.section_context: Indian Subcontinent's shifting names, boundaries, ancient identity, and sources
periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's central inquiry — how a land acquires names from within and without — so the physical map and the name-sorting task give students an early stake in the evidence. A common confusion is that 'India' has always been the country's official name; the map activity makes clear that the Subcontinent's boundaries and labels have shifted over millennia.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can frame questions about how and why place-names change across historical periods.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can sort name-evidence by likely source type and justify their classification.

periods.activity_title: Sapta Sindhava: Reading the Rig Veda's Regional Name
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Rig Veda and 'Sapta Sindhava'
materials: Blackboard
Printed or written extract: Rig Veda reference to 'Sapta Sindhava'
periods.visual_aids: Simple sketch-map on the board marking the Indus/Sindhu and the northwest region

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'Sapta Sindhava' on the board and asks students to break it into parts: 'Sapta' (seven), 'Sindhu' (river/Indus), 'ava' (suffix for land of). Students deduce the meaning — 'land of the seven rivers' — and identify the root word Sindhu. Teacher explains that this name appears in the Rig Veda, India's oldest text, several thousand years old, as a reference to the northwest part of the Subcontinent only.

Students read the short Rig Veda passage together and answer three written questions: (1) Which river does 'Sindhu' name? (2) Why is this a regional name, not a name for all of India? (3) What does it tell us that the oldest surviving Indian text names a river-region rather than a whole country? Students write their answers individually before a brief pair-share.

Teacher draws the chain on the board: Sindhu (river name) → Sapta Sindhava (region named after rivers) and asks students to think about what this naming logic reveals about how people formed identities around rivers. Small groups of three discuss: 'Can you think of any region near you that is named after a river or a natural feature?' Groups share one example each.

Quick write: each student completes one sentence — 'The Rig Veda calls the northwest region Sapta Sindhava, which means _______, and this name is [regional/national] because _______.' Teacher uses four or five read-alouds to check that the distinction between regional and whole-Subcontinent names is clear before closing.

periods.section_context: Rig Veda, 'Sapta Sindhava', Sindhu River, northwest region, regional identity
periods.teacher_notes: The Rig Veda material establishes that the earliest named Indian source gives only a regional label, not a name for the whole Subcontinent — a distinction that the rest of this chapter's Indian-naming section builds on. Students often conflate 'Sindhu' the river with 'Sindhu' meaning rivers in general; clarify that the word had both the specific and the general sense in early usage. The river-naming discussion connects to the physical map from the introductory activity, reinforcing that geography shaped early naming.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain why early Indian names were regional rather than whole-Subcontinent, tracing the logic of river-based naming.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can extract specific geographical and historical claims from an ancient text and evaluate what they do and do not tell us.

periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Mahabharata regional names and Fig. 5.4
materials: Printed or projected copy of Fig. 5.4 (Mahabharata-era regional map)
Blank outline map of the Indian Subcontinent (one per student)
Pencils/coloured pencils
periods.visual_aids: Fig. 5.4 — map of Mahabharata-era regions across the Subcontinent

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays Fig. 5.4 and explains that the Mahabharata, one of India's most celebrated texts composed from a few centuries BCE onward, lists numerous named regions across the Subcontinent. Students scan the map and call out names they recognise from present-day India — Kashmira, Kerala, Vanga, Kaccha — while teacher notes their modern equivalents on the board: Kashmir, Kerala, Bengal, Kutch.

Students receive a blank outline map of the Subcontinent and, using Fig. 5.4 as reference, locate and label at least five Mahabharata-era regions, placing a small bracket to show their approximate modern equivalent. They then answer in writing: 'What does the fact that the Mahabharata names regions in the north, south, east, and west tell us about what the text's authors understood about the Subcontinent's extent?'

Pairs compare maps and their written answers, then discuss: 'Is a text that lists regional names the same kind of source as one that names the whole Subcontinent? What is the difference in what each source tells us?' Pairs record one point of agreement and one remaining question.

Teacher draws out the key analytical point: the Mahabharata shows awareness of the whole Subcontinent by naming its parts, even though it also uses whole-Subcontinent terms — which will be the next focus. Students write one closing sentence: 'The Mahabharata's list of regional names tells us that ancient Indians [knew/did not know] the full extent of the Subcontinent because _______.'

periods.section_context: Mahabharata regional names — Kashmira, Vanga, Kerala, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha, Fig. 5.4
periods.teacher_notes: Having established in the Rig Veda unit that early naming was regional, this unit shows that the Mahabharata expands that regional awareness to cover the whole Subcontinent through a list of named parts. A common confusion is treating Fig. 5.4's regional names as exact equivalents of modern states; stress that boundaries were approximate and fluid. The map-labelling task is the core cognitive move — students must connect ancient names to physical locations, not just copy them.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can use a historical map to show how regional naming in ancient texts reflected expanding geographical awareness over time.

competency_edges.competency_text: Mapping textual geographical descriptions onto physical geography
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can locate ancient regional names on a physical outline map and match them to approximate modern equivalents.

periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, and Ashoka's inscription
materials: Blackboard
Short written excerpt: Mahabharata passage using 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa'
Brief note on Ashoka and the Pillar Inscription

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa' on the board and asks students to attempt a breakdown: 'Bharata + varsha' (country of the Bharatas) and 'Jambu + dvipa' (island of the jamun fruit). Teacher explains: 'Bharata' first appears in the Rig Veda as one of the main Vedic people, and several kings named Bharata appear in later literature; 'Jambudvipa' uses the jamun tree — native to the Subcontinent — as a geographical marker.

Students read the Mahabharata passage and a short note explaining that Emperor Ashoka (c. 250 BCE) used 'Jambudvipa' in an inscription to describe the whole of India — including what are today Bangladesh, Pakistan, and parts of Afghanistan. They then answer in writing: (1) What is the difference in meaning between 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa' as names? (2) Why is it significant that a king's inscription, not just a literary text, uses this name? (3) What does Ashoka's use of 'Jambudvipa' suggest about the boundaries of 'India' in 250 BCE?

Small groups compare answers to question 3 and debate: 'Does Ashoka's use of a single name for his territory mean the Subcontinent was politically unified, or only that people thought of it as a single geographical unit?' Each group prepares a one-sentence conclusion distinguishing political unity from geographical naming.

Groups share conclusions; teacher draws out the distinction on the board: a name for a territory and political control over it are different kinds of claims. Students record the key etymologies — Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa — and the Ashoka date as an anchor in their notes.

periods.section_context: Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, Mahabharata whole-Subcontinent terms, Ashoka inscription c. 250 BCE
periods.teacher_notes: Building on the regional names in the Mahabharata, this unit moves to the same text's whole-Subcontinent vocabulary — a significant shift that the Ashoka inscription then corroborates as real governmental usage. Students frequently confuse 'naming the Subcontinent' with 'ruling it'; the structured debate question is designed to surface and resolve that conflation. The Ashoka inscription is particularly valuable as an epigraphic source distinct from literary texts, so highlight that distinction explicitly.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between regional and whole-Subcontinent naming conventions and trace how whole-Subcontinent terms emerged across literary and epigraphic sources.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare what a literary text and a stone inscription each tell us, and identify the different kinds of authority each source carries.

periods.activity_title: 'Bharata' in the Vishnu Purana: A Geographical Definition
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Vishnu Purana verse and geographical boundaries
materials: Printed or board-written Sanskrit verse from the Vishnu Purana (with translation)
Physical map of the Indian Subcontinent
periods.visual_aids: Physical map of the Indian Subcontinent with the Himalayas and Indian Ocean marked

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the Vishnu Purana verse in translation: 'The country that lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is called Bharata.' Students identify the two boundary markers — 'the ocean' to the south and 'the snowy mountains' to the north — and locate both on the physical map.

The 'Think About It' activity: students answer three questions in writing. (1) What are the 'snowy mountains'? (2) Which ocean lies to the south? (3) Is this a complete geographical description of the Subcontinent — what boundaries does it leave out? Students annotate the map by drawing a rough southern boundary (ocean) and northern boundary (Himalayas) and noting what the verse says nothing about (eastern and western coasts).

Teacher introduces the ancient Tamil poem (c. 2,000 years ago) that describes a king's fame extending from Cape Kumari in the south to the great mountain in the north, and from the eastern ocean to the western ocean. Students compare the Tamil poem's description with the Vishnu Purana verse: which is more complete geographically? What does this comparison tell us about how authors in different regions of India imagined the Subcontinent's extent?

Students write a short comparative paragraph (4–5 sentences) arguing which of the two sources — the Vishnu Purana or the Tamil poem — gives a more complete geographical boundary for 'Bharata', and explain what the existence of both sources in different languages tells us about the name 'Bharata' across regions.

periods.section_context: Vishnu Purana verse, 'Bharata', Himalayas, Indian Ocean, ancient Tamil poem, Cape Kumari
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced 'Bharata' through the Rig Veda and Mahabharata, this unit examines how the Vishnu Purana formalises the name with a geographical definition — and then tests that definition against a southern Tamil source. A common confusion is that the Vishnu Purana verse defines all four directions; the map annotation task makes students notice the verse is silent on east and west, which the Tamil poem fills in. The cross-regional and cross-linguistic comparison is the key analytical move: two sources from different language traditions converging on the same geographical idea.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how the name 'Bharata' was formalised with a geographical definition across texts from different regions and languages.

competency_edges.competency_text: Mapping textual geographical descriptions onto physical geography
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can translate a verse-based geographical description into boundaries on a physical map and evaluate its completeness.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare two geographically descriptive sources from different language traditions and evaluate what each reveals about ancient conceptions of the Subcontinent.

periods.activity_title: 'Bharat' in the Indian Constitution: Ancient Name, Modern State
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — 'Bharat' in the Indian Constitution
materials: Printed reproduction of the Indian Constitution's opening page (or projected image)
Blackboard
periods.visual_aids: Reproduction of the opening page of the Indian Constitution showing Article 1

time_bands.activity: Students examine the reproduction of the Constitution's opening page and locate the phrase in Article 1: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.' Teacher asks: 'Why would a modern constitutional document begin with an ancient name?' Students write a one-sentence prediction before discussion.

Teacher leads a structured discussion tracing the full arc of the name 'Bharat': first appearing as a people's name in the Rig Veda, expanding into a territorial name 'Bharatavarsha' in the Mahabharata, codified geographically in the Vishnu Purana, appearing in the Tamil tradition as 'Bharatam', and now enshrined in the Constitution. Students build a written timeline on paper with five entries: Rig Veda → Mahabharata → Vishnu Purana → Tamil poem → Constitution, each with a one-phrase note on how 'Bharata' appears in that source.

Students discuss in pairs: 'What does it mean that the Constitution uses both 'India' and 'Bharat' in the same sentence? Which audiences might each name speak to?' Pairs prepare a two-sentence answer to share.

Brief class discussion drawing out that 'India' and 'Bharat' in the Constitution reflect the chapter's two main organising sections — the name from within and the name from outside. Students write a closing sentence: 'The Constitution's first line uses two names because _______.'

periods.section_context: Indian Constitution Article 1, 'India that is Bharat', Bharat/Bharatam across north and south India
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced 'Bharata' through Vedic and post-Vedic sources, this unit brings the name into the present by showing it in the Constitution — the most authoritative modern Indian document. Students often treat the Constitution's language as arbitrary; the timeline task makes the continuity between ancient and modern usage visible and concrete. The dual-name question in the Constitution also previews the chapter's second section, making this a natural pivot unit.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a timeline showing how a name's meaning evolved from a people-group label to a constitutional name for a modern state.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify and explain the difference in authority and purpose between an ancient literary source and a constitutional document that uses the same name.

periods.activity_title: Sindhu Becomes 'Hind': Persian Naming of India
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Persian names: Hind, Hidu, Hindu
materials: Blackboard
Short printed extract: description of 6th-century BCE Persian campaign into the Indus region
periods.visual_aids: Etymology chain written on the board: Sindhu → Hindhu → Hind / Hindu

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the chain on the board — Sindhu → Hindhu → Hind / Hindu / Hidu — and explains that this visual chain shows how the Persian language handled the Indian name. The initial sound 'S' became 'H' in Old Persian because Persian scribes heard and recorded the Sindhu region's name through their own phonological system. Students copy the chain and annotate each step with a one-word explanation of what changed.

Students read the short extract describing the 6th-century BCE Persian campaign into the Indus region and answer in writing: (1) What was the Persian emperor's motivation for recording the name of this region? (2) What does the Persian use of 'Hindu' tell us about how foreign naming works — is it based on direct knowledge of the whole country, or on contact with one part of it? (3) The chapter states that 'Hindu' in ancient Persian usage is a purely geographical term. What evidence supports this claim?

Class discussion on question 3: what is the difference between a geographical name and a religious name? Teacher establishes clearly that the Persian term predates the religious meaning by many centuries and was adopted solely as a regional geographic label. Students note this explicitly in writing: 'In ancient Persian, 'Hindu' meant _______, not _______.'

Students evaluate the Persian source as a historical record: what kind of evidence is a royal Persian inscription, and what can and cannot we conclude from it about India at the time? Each student writes one claim the Persian evidence supports and one claim it cannot support.

periods.section_context: Persian emperor, 6th century BCE, Sindhu-to-Hindhu sound shift, 'Hindu' as geographical term
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter's second section opens here, shifting from Indian self-naming to foreign naming — and the Persians provide the root from which nearly all foreign names derive. A very common and significant confusion is that 'Hindu' as used by ancient Persians carries religious meaning; the written task in the third band is specifically designed to surface and correct this. Students should leave this unit able to explain the sound-shift from Sindhu to Hindu as a linguistic process, not a change in meaning.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how a name travels across languages and changes phonetically while retaining its root geographical meaning.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate what a foreign royal inscription tells us about how outsiders named India, and identify the limits of that evidence.

periods.activity_title: From 'Hindhu' to 'Indoi': How the Greeks Named India
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Greek names: Indoi, Indike
materials: Blackboard
Etymology chain: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indoi/Indike
periods.visual_aids: Etymology chain on the board comparing Persian and Greek derivations from Sindhu

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes both chains on the board side by side — the Persian (Sindhu → Hindhu → Hind/Hindu) and the Greek (Sindhu → Hindhu → Indoi/Indike) — and asks students: 'What is the difference between the Persian and Greek versions? What happened to the 'H' in Greek?' Students notice that Greek dropped the initial 'H' because that sound did not exist in ancient Greek phonology.

Students work in pairs on a structured comparison: (1) Both Persian and Greek names derive from the same root — Sindhu. How does knowing this change your understanding of what 'India' means as a word? (2) Persian contact with India came through a military campaign in the 6th century BCE; how might Greek contact have been different, and what might that change about what Greeks knew of the Subcontinent? Students write their answers before sharing.

Teacher explains that from 'Indike' the Romans derived 'India', and from 'India' came many European languages' names for the Subcontinent. Students predict what Arabic, French, and Latin names for India might look like and record their predictions, then discuss how a single river name could generate a whole family of foreign names for an entire Subcontinent.

Students fill in the first three rows of the names table (Persian, Greek, Latin) based on the etymologies studied, writing the name, its root, and a one-phrase explanation of how the sound changed. This is the beginning of the 'Let's Explore' table from the chapter.

periods.section_context: Greek 'Indoi'/'Indike', drop of initial H, Persian-Greek derivation comparison, Roman 'India'
periods.teacher_notes: Having established the Persian derivation in the previous unit, this unit shows how the Greek borrowed and adapted the Persian form — demonstrating that naming is a chain of contact, not independent invention. Students sometimes think the Greeks knew Sanskrit and derived 'Indike' directly from 'Sindhu'; make clear that the Greek borrowed from Persian intermediaries. The partial table-filling task at the close is a concrete production that will be completed in the Chinese naming unit.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace a multi-step chain of name transmission across languages and identify what phonological rule governs each step.

periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Chinese names: Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu
materials: Blackboard
Short printed note on Chinese contact with India and the two Chinese names
Partial names table started in previous activity (or fresh copy)
periods.visual_aids: Etymology chain on the board: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indu → Yindu

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the Chinese chain: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indu → Yindu/Yintu. Students compare it to the Persian and Greek chains already on record and identify the common ancestor (Hindhu/Indu) and the point at which the Chinese path diverges. Teacher then introduces 'Tianzhu': derived from 'Sindhu' but also readable as 'heavenly master', reflecting Chinese reverence for India as the birthplace of the Buddha.

Students read the short note on Chinese contact with India — focusing on the Buddhist connection — and answer in writing: (1) Why would ancient Chinese travellers come to India? (2) What does the double meaning of 'Tianzhu' (geographical + reverential) tell us about the nature of Chinese contact with India? (3) How is the Chinese naming of India both similar to and different from the Persian naming? Students compare in pairs after writing.

Students complete the Chinese rows in their names table (Yindu/Yintu and Tianzhu) and then add the Arabic, English, and French rows based on the etymology chains studied across these units. For each completed row they write: the name, the root, and one sentence explaining the contact or sound change that produced it.

Three students share their completed rows for Arabic, English, and French; class corrects errors collaboratively. Teacher closes by noting that every foreign name in the table ultimately traces back to one Indian river name — Sindhu — a striking fact students record as the unit's closing statement.

periods.section_context: Chinese 'Yindu'/'Yintu'/'Tianzhu', Buddhist contact, Sindhu etymology chain completed
periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through Persian and Greek naming, students here complete the family of foreign names by adding the Chinese branch — which is significant because it introduces the Buddhist cultural connection alongside the geographical one. A common confusion is treating 'Tianzhu' as purely religious; stress that it began as a geographical derivation and acquired reverential resonance through Buddhist contact. The completed names table is the unit's tangible product and a revision tool.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can complete a multi-language etymology table showing how one root word generated distinct foreign names through different cultural contact routes.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural and religious influence on other civilisations
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how India's cultural reach shaped how ancient China named and understood the Subcontinent.

periods.activity_title: Xuanzang: A Pilgrim as a Historical Source
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Xuanzang sidebar ('Don't Miss Out')
materials: Short printed biography of Xuanzang (based on 'Don't Miss Out' box)
Blackboard

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the 'Don't Miss Out' profile of Xuanzang: a Chinese pilgrim who travelled to India in the 7th century CE, spent 17 years visiting scholars and sacred sites, collected Buddhist texts, and returned to China to translate Sanskrit manuscripts into Chinese. Students note three facts: the duration of his stay (17 years), his purpose (collecting Buddhist texts), and his output (Chinese translations of Sanskrit manuscripts).

Students answer in writing: (1) What kind of historical source is Xuanzang's travel record — primary or secondary, and why? (2) What can a pilgrim's account tell us that a royal inscription cannot? (3) What might Xuanzang's account be unable to tell us? Students discuss answers in pairs, then the class shares the most interesting contrast between a pilgrim account and an inscription.

Students role-play a structured scenario: they are historians who have found Xuanzang's travel account. They must decide: 'Which of the following claims could Xuanzang's account support? (a) India was a centre of Buddhist learning in the 7th century CE. (b) All Indians were Buddhist. (c) Indian and Chinese cultures were in contact. (d) The Sanskrit language was understood only in India.' Students classify each as 'supported', 'not supported', or 'uncertain', and give a one-phrase reason for each.

Teacher ties the Xuanzang unit back to the naming context: Xuanzang's visit is exactly the kind of cultural contact that shaped how China named India ('Tianzhu' — heavenly master). Students write one connecting sentence: 'Xuanzang's journey helps explain why the Chinese name 'Tianzhu' carries a reverential meaning because _______.'

periods.section_context: Xuanzang, 7th century CE, 17 years in India, Buddhist texts, Sanskrit-to-Chinese translation
periods.teacher_notes: Building on the Chinese naming unit's introduction of Xuanzang's reverential name for India, this unit examines Xuanzang himself as a historical source — the pilgrim account as a distinctive kind of evidence. Students often treat all old texts as equally reliable without thinking about the author's purpose and position; the classification task is designed to build that critical-source habit. The closing sentence explicitly links the source-evaluation work back to the naming strand so the two threads of the chapter remain connected.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate a pilgrim's travel account as a historical source by identifying what it can and cannot establish as evidence.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural and religious influence on other civilisations
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can use Xuanzang's account to explain how India's role as a centre of Buddhist learning shaped cultural exchange with ancient China.

periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — 'Hindustan' in Persian inscription, c. 1,800 years ago
materials: Blackboard
Short printed extract: reference to 'Hindustan' in a Persian inscription approximately 1,800 years ago

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces 'Hindustan' — derived from 'Hindu' (Persian for the Sindhu region) + 'stan' (Persian suffix meaning land or country) — and explains that this term appears in a Persian inscription approximately 1,800 years ago, and subsequently became the name most commonly used by invaders of India. Students note the construction: Hindu + stan = land of the Hindu (Sindhu) region, connecting it to the earlier Persian etymology chain.

Students read the short extract and answer in writing: (1) How is 'Hindustan' structurally different from 'Hind' or 'Hindu' — what does the suffix '-stan' add? (2) The chapter says 'Hindustan' became the term most commonly used by 'invaders'. What does that word choice tell us about how this name was used? (3) How does the name 'Hindustan' compare to 'Bharatavarsha' in terms of who coined each and what they were trying to describe?

Students discuss question 3 in groups of three, then each group formulates a two-sentence answer to: 'Would you say 'Hindustan' and 'Bharatavarsha' are names for the same place? Explain what is the same and what is different about them.' Groups share with the class; teacher charts the comparison on the board.

Students write a closing paragraph (4–5 sentences) synthesising what they have learned about Persian naming: Hind/Hindu (6th century BCE) → Hindustan (approximately 1,800 years ago) → continued use by invaders. They explain what this sequence reveals about the relationship between naming and power.

periods.section_context: 'Hindustan', Persian suffix '-stan', c. 1,800-year-old inscription, use by invaders of India
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the Persian Sindhu→Hindu chain in an earlier unit, this unit completes the Persian strand by introducing 'Hindustan' as a later, fuller formation from the same root. A common confusion is treating 'Hindustan' as simply another word for 'India' without considering who coined it and in what context; the structured comparison with 'Bharatavarsha' makes the contrast between insider and outsider naming explicit. The paragraph task asks students to connect a sequence of names to a pattern — naming as a political act — which is one of the chapter's deeper analytical moves.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the development of 'Hindustan' from its Persian root and explain what its pattern of usage reveals about naming and power.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types as evidence
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare an insider literary name and an outsider inscriptional name for the same territory and evaluate what each source's origin tells us.

periods.activity_title: Completing the Names Table: Arabic, Latin, English, and French
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — full foreign-names table ('Let's Explore')
materials: Printed version of the 'Let's Explore' names table (rows: Persian, Greek, Latin, Chinese, Arabic and Persian, English, French)
Blackboard with etymology chains for reference
periods.visual_aids: Complete etymology chains for all foreign-name families displayed on the board

time_bands.activity: Students receive the full names table and work individually to complete any rows already studied (Persian, Greek, Chinese). Teacher then introduces the remaining rows — Latin ('India'), Arabic ('Hind'/'Al-Hind'), English ('India'), and French ('Inde') — tracing each to the Sindhu root through the chains on the board. Students fill in each row: name, root, and the route through which the language received it.

Students work in pairs to answer three analytical questions about the completed table: (1) Which languages borrowed the name from Persian, and which from Greek or Latin? (2) Do any names in the table come from a root other than Sindhu? (3) What does it tell us that every foreign name for India traces to one river in the northwest of the Subcontinent? Pairs write a combined answer of 3–4 sentences.

Groups of four compare their analytical answers and produce a group consensus statement of two sentences: 'What the names table proves about how India was known to the outside world.' Groups share; teacher records key phrases on the board, drawing out that foreign knowledge of India was geographically partial — anchored to the northwest — even as Indian self-knowledge extended to the full Subcontinent.

Students write one synthesis sentence connecting the table to the chapter's organising question: 'Every foreign name in this table ultimately comes from _______, which shows that foreign naming of India was based on _______.'

periods.section_context: Full foreign-names table — Latin, Arabic, English, French, all deriving from Sindhu root
periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through each foreign naming tradition individually in earlier units, this unit consolidates them by completing the full comparative table — the chapter's own 'Let's Explore' activity. Students sometimes assume Arabic names come from a different root; confirm that 'Al-Hind' is a straightforward Arabic adaptation of the Persian 'Hind'. The group consensus statement about geographical partiality is the analytical payoff of the whole foreign-names section.

periods.activity_title: Two Naming Traditions: A Whole-Chapter Synthesis
materials: Blackboard
Blank two-column comparison frame (paper or board): 'Names from Within' | 'Names from Outside'
periods.visual_aids: Completed two-column comparison frame built on the board collaboratively

time_bands.activity: Students independently populate a two-column frame — 'Names from Within India' and 'Names from Outside India' — drawing on all the sources the chapter introduced: Rig Veda (Sapta Sindhava), Mahabharata (Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa), Ashoka's inscription (Jambudvipa), Vishnu Purana (Bharata), Tamil poem (Bharatam), Indian Constitution (Bharat) in the left column; Persian inscriptions (Hind/Hindu/Hindustan), Greek texts (Indoi/Indike), Latin (India), Chinese sources (Yindu, Tianzhu), Arabic (Al-Hind) in the right column. For each entry they note: the source type, approximate date or period, and the geographical scope implied by the name.

Using the completed frame, students write responses to three comparative questions: (1) Indian names for the Subcontinent moved from regional (Sapta Sindhava) to whole-Subcontinent (Bharatavarsha, Bharata) over time — what drove that expansion? (2) Foreign names for India were geographically anchored to the northwest throughout — why, and what does that reveal about the nature of early foreign contact with the Subcontinent? (3) Both 'Bharat' and 'India' appear in the Constitution's first line — which naming tradition does each belong to, and why does the Constitution use both?

Students write a structured analytical paragraph (5–7 sentences) arguing: 'The way a people names a land tells us as much about the namer as it does about the land.' They must use at least three named sources from the chapter — one Indian, one foreign, one epigraphic or legal — as evidence. This is the synthesis writing task, begun and completed within this sitting: drafting, a one-minute self-review for evidence inclusion, and a final version.

Three or four students read their paragraphs aloud. Class identifies: which sources were used most often, which argument appeared most frequently, and what a strong paragraph included that weaker ones missed. Teacher closes by returning to the chapter's title — 'India, That Is Bharat' — and asking students to explain in one sentence why those two names sit together in the same phrase.

periods.section_context: All chapter sources synthesised: Sapta Sindhava, Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, Bharata, Hind, Indoi, Yindu, Tianzhu, Hindustan, Constitution
periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the chapter's two main naming traditions — Indian and foreign — by asking students to use sources from across the chapter as evidence in a structured argument. The three comparative questions are designed to surface the two key analytical insights: that Indian naming expanded inward from region to whole, and that foreign naming stayed anchored to the northwest throughout. The paragraph task is self-contained — students draft and self-review within this sitting — and the peer evaluation at the close gives every student a model of strong evidence use.

assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — Rig Veda and 'Sapta Sindhava'
assessment_items.question_text: The Rig Veda calls the northwest part of the Indian Subcontinent 'Sapta Sindhava'. Which of the following best explains why this is a regional name rather than a name for all of India?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a foreign name given by Persian travellers who only visited the northwest.

options.label: B
options.text: It refers to the seven rivers of the northwest, naming one geographical zone, not the whole Subcontinent.

options.label: C
options.text: It was a name used only by kings, so it could not apply to the whole Subcontinent.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rig Veda was written after the Mahabharata, when India had not yet been explored fully.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the Persian naming tradition with the Rig Veda, mixing up the chapter's two main sections.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the chronological relationship between the Rig Veda and the Mahabharata.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a social-restriction explanation not present in the chapter; misreads 'regional' as 'elite'.

assessment_items.chapter_section: How Foreigners Named India — 'Hindustan' in Persian inscription, c. 1,800 years ago
assessment_items.question_text: The name 'Hindustan' appears in a Persian inscription about 1,800 years ago and became the name most commonly used by invaders of India. What does the origin and pattern of use of this name most clearly reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that ancient Indians preferred the name 'Hindustan' over 'Bharata' for official purposes.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that 'Hindustan' replaced 'Hind' because invaders wanted a shorter name for daily use.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that outsiders named India based on their point of contact — the Sindhu/northwest — and that naming can reflect a relationship of conquest.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that the Persian language had no existing word for India and needed to invent one from scratch.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reverses the insider/outsider distinction; ancient Indians used 'Bharata', not 'Hindustan', for their own land.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Ignores the etymology chain showing 'Hindustan' was built from the existing Persian word 'Hindu' plus the suffix '-stan'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Invents a convenience explanation with no textual basis; also gets the direction of change wrong — 'Hindustan' is longer than 'Hind'.

assessment_items.chapter_section: How Foreigners Named India — Chinese names: Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu
assessment_items.task: Complete the cause-effect map below. In the centre box write the root name from which all foreign names for India derive. Then, for each of the four named languages — Persian, Greek, Chinese, and Arabic — fill in: (a) the name that language uses for India, and (b) a brief note on the contact route or sound change that produced it. Finally, in the 'What this shows' box, write one sentence explaining what the pattern across all four branches reveals about how early foreign knowledge of India was formed.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Centre box: Root name → _______ 
Persian branch: Name → _______  |  Contact/change → _______
Greek branch: Name → _______  |  Contact/change → _______
Chinese branch: Name → _______  |  Contact/change → _______
Arabic branch: Name → _______  |  Contact/change → _______
What this shows: _______
format_of_output: A completed cause-effect map with the root name in the centre, four branches each with a name and a contact/change note, and one concluding sentence in the 'What this shows' box.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find diagrammatic formats difficult may respond in a numbered list with the same five entries. The teacher may read the scaffold aloud for students with reading difficulties.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate that they can organise etymology knowledge into a visual causal structure, showing the single root (Sindhu) and its divergent paths through different cultural contact routes, and then generalise the pattern into a closing claim.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students through the centre-to-branch structure of a cause-effect map. Each branch has two parts — the name and the mechanism — so students must recall both the outcome (the foreign name) and the process (how contact or phonology produced it). The final 'What this shows' box asks for synthesis, not just recall.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Sindhu correctly placed in the centre; all four branches accurately completed; contact notes distinguish between direct borrowing (Arabic from Persian) and phonological change (S→H in Persian, drop of H in Greek); the concluding sentence makes a generalisation about geographical partiality of foreign knowledge. Weak: Only some branches completed; contact notes merely restate the name change without explaining the mechanism; the concluding sentence restates a single branch rather than generalising across the map.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because it requires students to show both the single root cause (Sindhu) and its multiple, distinct effects (the different foreign names) simultaneously — a linear list cannot capture the branching structure of etymology transmission. The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu, such as a comparison table with the same information in columns.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Introduction — India as an ancient land with changing names
assessment_items.question_text: A student is sorting names for India into two groups: 'names from texts written by people who lived in India' and 'names from texts or records made by outsiders'. Which of the following sortings is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 'Bharatavarsha' → names from inside India; 'Hind' → names from outside India.

options.label: B
options.text: 'Bharatavarsha' → names from outside India; 'Hind' → names from inside India.

options.label: C
options.text: Both 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Hind' → names from inside India, because both are old names.

options.label: D
options.text: Both 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Hind' → names from outside India, because both derive from 'Sindhu'.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Reverses the insider/outsider distinction entirely; likely confuses the Persian and Indian naming traditions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies an age criterion ('both are old') instead of an origin criterion; fails to distinguish between who produced each name.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Correctly notes both derive from 'Sindhu' but draws the wrong conclusion — 'Bharatavarsha' derives from 'Bharata' (a people name), not from 'Sindhu'.

assessment_items.question_text: Xuanzang, a Chinese pilgrim, spent 17 years in India in the 7th century CE, visiting scholars and collecting Buddhist texts. A historian wants to use Xuanzang's account as evidence. Which claim is best supported by this source?

options.label: B
options.text: India was a significant centre of Buddhist learning that attracted long-distance scholarly travel in the 7th century CE.

options.label: C

what_each_option_reveals.C: Makes an absolute claim about Sanskrit literacy that goes beyond what the source supports; Xuanzang's translation work shows Chinese could engage with Sanskrit, not that no one could before him.

options.text: Kashmira → Assam; Vanga → Kutch; Kaccha → Kashmir.

options.label: B
options.text: Kashmira → Kashmir; Vanga → Bengal; Kaccha → Kutch.

options.text: Kashmira → Kerala; Vanga → Assam; Kaccha → Bengal.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Mahabharata Regional Name | Approximate Location on Fig. 5.4
Kashmira | Far northwest, near the Himalayas
Vanga | Eastern coast, near the delta region
Pragjyotisha | Far northeast
Kaccha | Western peninsula
Kerala | Far southwest
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may refer to a physical map of India while answering this question.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses eastern and southern locations; likely has not cross-referenced the map with modern state names.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Scrambles all three pairings; shows a general failure to map textual names onto geographical locations.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Swaps Kashmira and Vanga while also misplacing Kaccha; suggests confusion between northwest and east.

competency.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural and religious influence on other civilisations

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how India's cultural reach shaped how ancient China named and understood the Subcontinent.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Foreigners Named India — Chinese names: Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu
assessment_items.question_text: The ancient Chinese used two names for India: 'Yindu' (derived from the Sindhu root) and 'Tianzhu' (also derived from Sindhu, but readable as 'heavenly master'). What best explains why 'Tianzhu' carries a reverential meaning while 'Yindu' does not?

options.label: A
options.text: Chinese contact with India was shaped by Buddhism, so India was also seen as the land of the Buddha — giving the name a sacred resonance beyond its geographical root.

options.label: B
options.text: Chinese emperors renamed India 'Tianzhu' as a political tribute to acknowledge India's military power.

options.label: C
options.text: 'Tianzhu' is a translation of 'Bharata', which also means 'heavenly' in Sanskrit.

options.label: D
options.text: 'Yindu' was used only by ordinary people, while 'Tianzhu' was the official government name with no religious meaning.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Invents a Sanskrit etymology for 'Tianzhu' that is not in the chapter; confuses the Chinese name with the Indian naming tradition.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Substitutes a military explanation for a cultural/religious one; contradicts the chapter's account of Xuanzang and Buddhist pilgrimage.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fabricates a social-register distinction (popular vs. official) with no basis in the chapter; also incorrectly strips the religious meaning from 'Tianzhu'.
